prize_parts.citation: for the discovery of room-temperature tunnel magnetoresistance in magnetic tunnel junctions and its development into a large effect with crystalline barriers

statement.case_for: B005 fits the mandate as I read it: an original experiment, unambiguous and verified, with a measurable consequence that matters beyond the laboratory. The 1995 observations of sizeable tunnel magnetoresistance at room temperature by Moodera and by Miyazaki, independently and almost simultaneously, turned Julliere's low-temperature curiosity into a usable effect. The later giant TMR in MgO-barrier junctions, where coherent tunnelling through a crystalline barrier was confirmed experimentally, made it a real device principle in read heads, sensors and MRAM. It has been reproduced worldwide for three decades and the interpretation is stable. Nothing here is premature, and I would rather honour a finished, verified discovery than a field still working out what it has found. I also take Moodera and Miyazaki as the original experimenters on the record, which is the point I care most about when I ask who did the work first.
statement.case_against: The strongest reservation is Olle Eriksson's: after the 2007 prize for giant magnetoresistance, TMR can be read as an incremental, device-oriented sequel. The credited names are also imperfect. Yuasa and the Djayaprawira group had the MgO giant effect in parallel with Parkin, and the theoretical prediction of coherent MgO tunnelling (Butler, Mathon) is outside what the prize can represent with three people. Parkin's name rests on the MgO step rather than the 1995 discovery, so the citation has to be written carefully or the attribution is open to challenge. This candidate has little support in the opening ballots (only Olle and I ranked it), and I should say honestly that this reflects a field the committee has partly credited already.

responses.point: Olle ranks B005 fourth but worries that it is incremental after the 2007 GMR prize and that the MgO credit is split among people not on the list, including Yuasa and the theorists Butler and Mathon.
responses.response: The worry about the credit split is fair, and it is why I would keep the citation anchored on the 1995 room-temperature discovery, which belongs clearly to Moodera and Miyazaki, rather than on MgO alone. I do not agree that it is merely incremental: GMR is a metallic multilayer effect, whereas TMR is a different physical mechanism, spin-dependent tunnelling, with a larger signal, and the original experiment was not a variation on Fert and Grunberg. Where I accept his point is that Parkin's inclusion rests on a later step, and I would want the committee to check the 2004 priority question against Yuasa before we commit to a three-person list. His own candidate B021 is my second choice, so the disagreement is one of timing and of what has been settled, not of principle.

responses.point: Stefan puts the optical lattice clocks (B024) first as a measurement instrument that redefines what can be measured, with Katori and Ye as a clean two-person pair and multiple independent labs confirming 10^-18 performance.
responses.response: I sympathise strongly with the instrument argument, and B024 is on my own list. My reservation is the nature of the output: so far the clocks yield limits and a pending redefinition of the second, not a discovery about nature, and the prize sits close to 2005 for the frequency comb and 2012 for ion control. Stefan's own uncertainty about allocation between Katori's conception and Ye's performance also matters to me, since the prize is for the original idea and its first realisation, not for pushing a technique to its best number. If the committee wants a measurement-technology prize I would accept B024 as an alternative, but I think B005 has a more concrete verified effect and a broader consequence outside physics.

responses.point: Eva Lindroth ranks B020 first (ultracold atoms in optical lattices turned textbook Hubbard models into controllable systems) and B024 second, while admitting uncertainty about which three of five credited names should be chosen.
responses.response: I respect the scientific clarity of B020, but the attribution concern she raises is exactly where I hesitate: five credited names, a theory proposal by Jaksch and Zoller, the Mott experiment by Greiner and Bloch with Hansch not on the list, and fermionic work by Esslinger, so any trio omits someone with a real claim to the original work. Several colleagues also call the programme still maturing, since the payoff for open problems such as the doped Hubbard model is not yet reached. I would ask her whether she sees a single original experiment that the citation can name, rather than a field of simulation. If she does, that would raise B020 in my view.

responses.point: Mark ranks IceCube (B052, Halzen alone) first as a detector-driven discovery opening neutrino astronomy, with a single credited name that may not reflect who built the instrument.
responses.response: I agree with the principle that a new instrument that opens a door is what I look for, and the 2013 detection of cosmic neutrinos is solid. But the attribution is where I cannot be absolutely sure: a one-name prize for a large collaboration experiment, with the credit string unable to name the instrument builders, is the kind of configuration I would not want to rest on. Mark himself says he cannot verify the division of credit, and source identification is still only moderately significant for several associations. I would prefer to leave B052 until the committee has settled who did the original work.

uncertainties: Whether the committee accepts TMR as sufficiently distinct from the 2007 GMR prize.
Priority between Parkin and the Yuasa and Djayaprawira groups for the large MgO-barrier effect, and how to treat the Butler and Mathon theory.
Whether a prize centred on the 1995 discovery should credit only Moodera and Miyazaki, with Parkin on a separate or no part.
Whether B021 is mature enough, given the unsettled pairing mechanism in twisted bilayer graphene and the Cao and parallel-group credit.
My knowledge of the detailed history is from memory and is not verified.
statement.conflict_note: No specific conflict is apparent from my profile for B005. I have no known connection to Moodera, Miyazaki or Parkin. Göran Johansson is a Chalmers colleague, but he is not tied to this candidate. I have collaborated on TEM work with Japanese microscopy communities, which is not a connection to Miyazaki or to any shortlisted candidate. If B016 or B021 came to the front I would check for overlap with co-authors, though none is evident.
